chapter: Failure in St. Louis and the Omaha bands
title: Buck Clayton in Parsons and Charlie Parker in Kansas City, Kansas
summary: Jam session with Buck Clayton, home from Count Basie's band, showed Thompson that jazz musicians were gentlemen; he also recalls hearing Charlie Parker in Kansas City.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: And that's where I really got introduced to jazz formally by Wilbur, W-i-l-b-u-r, known as Buck, B-u-c-k, last name Clayton, C-l-a-y-t-o-n.
Now, Sir Charles, what did Buck mean to you, where did you meet him, and what came off that meeting?

I met Buck Clayton in Parsons, Kansas at a house right down the street from where we lived. And there was a girl there who had a piano and she was not a good pianist but she was interested in music, and several of the guys in the neighborhood, including myself, were interested in her. And in that town Buck Clayton had come home to visit his parents. His father was a minister in that town, and there was another famous musician whose name was Bill Davis, the organist. His father was a minister there, and we were all in this town at the same time, and so we had a jam session at this girls' house, and Buck played. He had just come back from China not too long before that and he had joined Count Basie's band which was playing Kansas City at this time.

Now, what I forgot to tell you was during a period of my school days I had been going to school in Kansas City,

Kansas, which was just across the river from Kansas City, Missouri. And I had met Charlie Parker at that time who became famous later. And I had heard a lot of these jazz musicians and I got this sound in my ear, you know. I didn't go in the night clubs but I had heard these musicians at jam sessions. And that's when Charlie Parker started out.

And so I had had this association in Kansas City, Kansas with the Kansas City music, which was the real music of the night life crowd, which later on became so famous with Count Basie. So Buck Clayton was working with Count Basie, and I was so impressed with his playing and his looks. He was a very, very clean, intelligent man who convinced me that jazz musicians were also gentlemen and intelligent people, not necessarily the drunks that people had thought that they were -- all were.
And so in other words I didn't think that I'd be going too far away from my keeping to play music, because Buck Clayton happened to be the son of a minister too and was doing very well.
